The oomycetes ( / ˌ oʊ . ə ˈ m aɪ s iː t s / ), [ 2 ] or Oomycota , form a distinct phylogenetic lineage of fungus -like eukaryotic microorganisms within the Stramenopiles . They are filamentous and heterotrophic , and can reproduce both sexually and asexually . Sexual reproduction of an oospore is the result of contact between hyphae of male antheridia and female oogonia ; these spores can overwinter and are known as resting spores. [ 3 ] : 409 Asexual reproduction involves the formation of chlamydospores and sporangia , producing motile zoospores . [ 3 ] Oomycetes occupy both saprophytic and pathogenic lifestyles, and include some of the most notorious pathogens of plants, causing devastating diseases such as late blight of potato and sudden oak death . One oomycete, the mycoparasite Pythium oligandrum , is used for biocontrol , attacking plant pathogenic fungi. [ 4 ] The oomycetes are also often referred to as water molds (or water moulds ), although the water-preferring nature which led to that name is not true of most species, which are terrestrial pathogens.
